notes.title: Start here: an analytics backend in eight ADRs
notes.body:
pulse-net is a product-analytics backend in the style of PostHog: events come in through `POST /capture`, get attached to persons, and are answered by a query engine, feature flags and exports. It has three projects: `Pulse.Domain` (pure logic, no packages), `Pulse.Infrastructure` (EF Core on SQLite and the services) and `Pulse.Api` (endpoints, auth and the two background workers).

Read `docs/architecture.md` first, then the ADRs in `docs/adr/` in order. Every ADR ends with two useful sections:

- **In the code** gives file and line pointers. Open each one; the quiz is about what those lines do.
- **Review notes** are a reviewer's claims about weak spots. Treat each one as a hypothesis and check it against the code yourself.

Each ADR also has a **Check:** exercise. Doing them is the best preparation for this quest.

excerpts.quote: pulse-net is a PostHog/Mixpanel-style product-analytics backend: events flow in through a durable ingestion pipeline,

readMore.why: The layer map and a section per subsystem.

notes.title: Concept: a durable queue with a doorbell
notes.body:
Capture does not write events directly. It appends rows to a `QueuedEvents` table and answers at once; a background worker processes the table later. Three general ideas help when reading this code.

- **Doorbell.** A `System.Threading.Channels` channel can carry a wake-up signal instead of data. Its capacity and `FullMode` decide what happens when someone rings while the reader is busy. Read both settings in `IngestionSignal`.
- **Delivery guarantees.** At-most-once means work can be lost but never repeated; at-least-once means it is never lost but can repeat; exactly-once needs a transaction or deduplication that covers both the work and the bookkeeping.
- **Dead letters.** A row that keeps failing is moved aside so it cannot block the rest.

What to look for in `IngestionProcessor.ProcessPendingAsync`: the order of the database calls in each `case`, which of them are separate statements, and how the `Attempts` counter is read, compared with `MaxAttempts` and copied into a `DeadLetterEvent`. Then read `IngestionWorker.DrainAsync` and note when it stops.

excerpts.quote: The wake-up is a bounded `Channel<bool>` of capacity 1 (`DropWrite`) used purely as a doorbell

notes.title: Concept: who may read, which bucket, which page
notes.body:
Three smaller subsystems round out the quest.

**Access.** HTTP has three different refusals: 401 (we do not know who you are), 403 (we know you, and you may not) and 404 (there is nothing here for you). Read `ProjectAccessService` and write down, for each method, which credential it looks at first and under what condition it looks at the other one. Then read the `ForwardDefaultSelector` in `Program.cs` and note the exact string comparison it uses.

**Flags.** `FeatureFlagHasher` turns a flag key and a user id into a number in [0, 1]. Look closely at every comparison operator in `IsInRollout` and `PickVariant`; boundary values are where they matter.

**Exports and time.** Exports page with a cursor instead of an offset. Read `EncodeCursor` and `TryDecodeCursor`, then follow the call up into `ExportEndpoints` and list each `try`/`catch` on the way. In `PulseDbContext`, read both lambdas of the ticks converter and ask what each one keeps.

excerpts.quote: Every management endpoint is scoped to a project by a GUID in the route.

notes.title: Why a query right after a 202 can miss the event
notes.body:
The capture handler adds one `QueuedEvent` per event, saves, rings the signal and returns 202. The `Events` row is written later by `IngestionWorker` through `CaptureService`. A query that runs before the worker has drained the queue does not see the event; reads are eventually consistent, and the ADR tells tests to poll the metrics endpoint until `pending` is 0.

- The 202 follows the save of the queue row, not of the event row.
- Capture no longer calls the ingest pipeline inside the request.
- There is no nightly batch; the worker runs continuously, woken by the signal or a 1-second sweep.

excerpts.quote: Reads are eventually consistent: a query issued immediately after a 202 may not see the event.

notes.title: Why fifty rings leave one signal
notes.body:
`IngestionSignal` builds `Channel.CreateBounded<bool>(new BoundedChannelOptions(1) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite })`. The channel holds one item. `Ring` calls `TryWrite`; when the channel is full, DropWrite discards the item being written. So after fifty rings during a busy drain, exactly one signal is waiting. That is enough, because the worker reads the table, not the signal.

- A capacity-1 channel cannot hold fifty items.
- Rows never wait for a restart: the worker also sweeps every second.
- `TryWrite` never blocks; it returns at once whether or not the item was kept.

notes.title: Three tries, but the dead letter says Attempts = 2
notes.body:
`Attempts` starts at 0. A transient failure returns Retry while `row.Attempts + 1 >= MaxAttempts` is false, and the Retry case writes `row.Attempts + 1`. So the first failure stores 1, the second stores 2, and the third sees 2 + 1 >= 3 and dead-letters. The `DeadLetterEvent` copies `Attempts = row.Attempts`, which is still 2, even though its error text says it failed after 3 attempts. The stored count is one lower than the real number of tries.

- Retries stop at the cap; there is no backoff at all.
- A fourth try never happens.
- Only missing projects and invalid payloads dead-letter at once; exceptions from ingest are transient.

excerpts.quote: return row.Attempts + 1 >= MaxAttempts ? (RowOutcome.DeadLettered, $"Failed after {MaxAttempts} attempts: {ex.Message}") : (RowOutcome.Retry, null);

notes.title: Why a crash can duplicate an event
notes.body:
In the Processed case, `CaptureService.IngestAsync` has already saved the event; only then does `DeleteRowAsync` run its own `ExecuteDeleteAsync`. These are two separate statements with no transaction around both. If the process dies between them, the queue row is still there on restart and is ingested again, producing a second copy of the event. The ADR names this at-least-once behavior and suggests a shared transaction or dedup by event id.

- Ingest and delete do not share a transaction.
- Nothing detects duplicates, so the row is not dead-lettered.
- The event was committed before the crash; nothing rolls it back.

excerpts.quote: A processed row is deleted in a separate statement after `CaptureService` has saved

notes.title: Why a non-member gets 404, not 403
notes.body:
`RequireMemberAsync` first reads the user id. Only a caller with no user id gets 401. For a signed-in caller it runs one `AnyAsync` over `ProjectMemberships` and returns `Results.NotFound()` when there is no row. That is the same response a project id that does not exist produces, so a non-member cannot tell real projects from fake ones.

- 403 would confirm the project exists; the API has no 403 in project routes.
- 401 is reserved for callers with no identity at all.
- The guard returns before any data is read, so there is no empty 200.

excerpts.quote: There is no 403 anywhere in the project-scoped API.

notes.title: Why a valid read key does not help a signed-in non-member
notes.body:
`RequireReadAsync` checks the `X-Api-Key` header only when the key is present **and** `GetUserId(http.User)` is null. A request that also carries a valid JWT has a user id, so the key branch is skipped and the method falls through to `RequireMemberAsync`. The user is not a member, so the answer is 404.

- The read key is never compared here, so it cannot grant access.
- The 401 Invalid read key result belongs to the key branch, which did not run.
- Nothing in this path returns 403.

notes.title: How one Bearer header reaches two handlers
notes.body:
The default scheme is a policy scheme whose `ForwardDefaultSelector` reads the Authorization header and calls `StartsWith` with `"Bearer "` plus `ApiKeyGenerator.PersonalPrefix`, using `StringComparison.Ordinal`. A match forwards to `PersonalApiKeyAuthenticationHandler`; everything else goes to JwtBearer. The prefix routes the request before any token is parsed or looked up.

- The selector never counts dots or parses a JWT.
- The hash lookup happens later, inside the personal-key handler.
- The comparison is ordinal (case-sensitive) and needs the full user prefix, not just `pk_`.

notes.title: What the ticks converter keeps and drops
notes.body:
On write the converter stores `v.UtcTicks`, a count of ticks for the instant in UTC. 10:00 at +02:00 is 08:00 UTC. On read it builds `new DateTimeOffset(v, TimeSpan.Zero)`, so the value comes back as 08:00 with offset +00:00: the same instant, without the original offset. ADR 0006 accepts this because all analytics math is in UTC.

- The +02:00 offset is not stored anywhere, so it cannot come back.
- The clock time is converted, not relabelled: 10:00 becomes 08:00.
- The column is an integer, so SQLite compares numbers, not text.

excerpts.quote: : base(v => v.UtcTicks, v => new DateTimeOffset(v, TimeSpan.Zero))
The original client offset is **not round-tripped**: everything reads back as `+00:00`.

notes.title: Why the out-of-range cursor still gets a 400
notes.body:
`TryDecodeCursor` parses -1 as a valid `long` and then calls `new DateTimeOffset(ticks, TimeSpan.Zero)`, which throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. Its own `catch (FormatException)` does not match, so the exception leaves `EventsPageAsync`. But the endpoint awaits that call inside `catch (ArgumentException)`, and in C# a catch clause also matches derived types: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` derives from `ArgumentException`. The endpoint returns `CursorProblem()`, a 400. ADR 0007's review note predicts the global handler; the code says otherwise.

- No 500 here: the exception is caught one level up.
- A bad cursor never restarts the scan.
- The membership guard ran earlier; the cursor error is a 400.

notes.title: Why an empty page can still have a next cursor
notes.body:
Property filters are opaque JSON to SQLite, so the export scans a page of rows by `(Timestamp, Id)` in SQL and filters them afterwards in memory. A page can lose some or all of its rows to the filter while the cursor still points at the last row scanned. Only a null cursor means the scan reached the end. The client should keep requesting pages.

- An empty page is not an end signal; null is.
- Nothing timed out; the filter simply matched no rows in this slice.
- Matching nothing is a valid result, not a 400.

excerpts.quote: so a filtered page may contain fewer than `limit` rows while the cursor still advances — the cursor tracks scan position, not result count.

notes.title: Why a position of exactly 50.0 picks test
notes.body:
`PickVariant` computes `position = Rank(..., VariantSalt) * 100` and walks the variants, adding each rollout to `cumulative` and returning the first variant where `position < cumulative`. For control, 50.0 < 50 is false. For test, cumulative is 100 and 50.0 < 100 is true, so the user gets test.

- The comparison is strict, so 50.0 is not inside control's range.
- There is no re-ranking on ties; the salt is fixed.
- Ties go to the later variant here, because of the strict comparison.

notes.title: Why 0% excludes even a rank of 0.0
notes.body:
`IsInRollout` short-circuits to true only when `rolloutPercentage >= 100`. Otherwise it returns `Rank(flagKey, distinctId) * 100 < rolloutPercentage`. With 0% and a rank of 0.0, that is 0 < 0, which is false, so the user is not in the rollout. Because the test is strict, a 0% flag excludes everyone.

- A rank of 0.0 is not special; it still has to be strictly below the percentage.
- 0% does not short-circuit; only 100% or more does.
- Variant selection runs only for users who pass the gate.
